back: Ensure the project includes all the work required, and only the work required. In the 8th edition it also covers the quality of the deliverables.
The features, functions and characteristics of the product, service or result.
The work performed to deliver a product, service or result with the specified features and functions.
A condition or capability that must be present in a product, service or result to satisfy a business need.
Plan Scope Management; Elicit and Analyze Requirements; Define Scope; Develop Scope Structure; Monitor and Control Scope; Validate Scope.
Describes HOW scope will be defined, developed, monitored, controlled and validated. Part of the project management plan, not of the scope baseline.
Describes how requirements will be analyzed, documented and managed, including prioritization and traceability.
Determining, documenting and managing stakeholder needs and requirements. Output: requirements documentation. Older name: Collect Requirements.
Functional: what the product does (behaviors, actions, data). Nonfunctional: how well it does it (performance, security, reliability).
Temporary capabilities needed to move from the current state to the future state, such as data conversion and training.
A grid that links each requirement from its origin to the deliverable that satisfies it. Tracks requirements through the life cycle and helps manage scope changes.
Brainstorming followed by a vote to rank the ideas.
Sorts a large number of ideas into groups for review and analysis.
Prequalified stakeholders and subject matter experts brought together to learn their expectations and attitudes about a proposed product or result.
Scope description, deliverables, acceptance criteria and project exclusions.

front: Project charter vs project scope statement
back: Charter: high level, authorizes the project. Scope statement: detailed description of scope and its boundaries, part of the scope baseline.
The set of conditions that must be met before deliverables are accepted.
A hierarchical decomposition of the total scope of work to be carried out by the team to meet the objectives and create the deliverables.
The lowest level of the WBS, with a unique identifier. Belongs to exactly one control account.
A management control point where scope, budget and schedule are integrated and compared with earned value. Contains two or more work packages.
A WBS component below the control account and above the work package, with known work content but no detailed schedule activities yet.
The document with detailed information about each WBS component: description of work, responsible organization, milestones, resources, cost estimates, acceptance criteria.
The WBS contains all product and project work, including project management. Nothing is left out and no extra work is included.
The technique of dividing and subdividing scope and deliverables into smaller, more manageable parts. Used to create the WBS.
Approved project scope statement + WBS + WBS dictionary. Changed only through formal change control.
The scope baseline, schedule baseline and cost baseline together.
Monitors scope status, manages changes to the scope baseline and measures deliverable quality. Output: verified deliverables. Older names: Control Scope, Control Quality.
Formalizes acceptance of completed deliverables by the customer or sponsor. Input: verified deliverables. Output: accepted deliverables.
Verified: the team has checked them for correctness. Accepted: the customer or sponsor has formally approved them. Verified comes first.
Uncontrolled expansion of scope without adjusting time, cost and resources.
The team adds extras the customer did not ask for. Not acceptable.
A dynamic, prioritized list of work items and features. In adaptive work it corresponds to the WBS.
A checklist of all the criteria a deliverable must meet to be considered ready for customer use.
